lines: A macro that races two separate pieces of work against each other and moves on as soon as whichever one finishes first.
What actually happens to the piece of work that loses that race?
answer: It gets dropped outright. Its whole future simply stops existing.
This isn't a pause, and it isn't something quietly finishing up in the background. It's gone, the instant the other one wins.

lines: Run it for real, and check back well after the losing side's own full delay should have passed anyway.
Its own side effect never happened at all — not late, not eventually. Dropped really does mean dropped.
Now take a channel receive call, cancel it partway through waiting with that same racing macro, then actually send a message and call receive again fresh.
Could that first message ever quietly go missing because of the cancelled attempt?
answer: No — nothing goes missing. This particular receive call is safe to cancel.
It either hasn't seen a message yet, or it's fully received one. There's no half-finished state in between for a cancellation to catch it in.

lines: Run it for real: after the cancelled attempt, a fresh receive call gets exactly the one message that was sent — nothing lost, nothing duplicated.
That's what makes a receive call like this one genuinely safe to use inside a racing macro, over and over, in a loop.
steps.takeaway: mpsc::Receiver::recv is cancel-safe — dropping it mid-wait and starting a fresh one loses nothing.

lines: Now try the same kind of cancellation on a different operation — one that reads an exact number of bytes from a stream, cancelled midway, after it's already pulled part of that data in.
What happens to the bytes it already grabbed before it got cancelled?
answer: They're simply gone. A fresh read only ever sees whatever arrives afterward.
Unlike the receive call, this operation genuinely has a half-finished state — and cancelling it catches that state and throws it away.

lines: Run it for real: the first half of what was sent, already pulled in by the cancelled read, never comes back. A fresh read only recovers the second half.
There's no mechanism in the language for handing that partial progress back anywhere once it's being dropped. It's simply lost, permanently.
steps.takeaway: read_exact is not cancel-safe — cancelling it mid-read loses the bytes it already consumed, permanently.

lines: Spawn a background task, get a handle back for it, and then drop that handle right away — without ever waiting on it, and without explicitly stopping the task.
Does the task actually stop running when its only handle disappears, or does it keep going?
answer: It keeps going completely. Dropping the handle only gives up the ability to check on it or wait for it.
That's a deliberate choice, not an oversight. A background task often needs to outlive whatever spawned it in the first place.

lines: Run it for real: long after that handle was dropped, the task is still quietly doing its work, completely unobserved by anything.
It was never cancelled at all. It simply became impossible to check on, or to stop through that particular handle.
So here's the same underlying mechanism, used three different ways, with three genuinely different outcomes.

A receive call drops cleanly and loses nothing. A partial read drops and loses exactly what it had already consumed. And a background task's handle drops while the task itself just keeps right on running.
steps.takeaway: Cancellation is always a drop at the current .await — whether that loses anything depends on what was paused.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: that racing macro genuinely drops whichever side loses, not merely delays it.
A channel receive call survives being cancelled with nothing lost. A partial stream read does not, and loses exactly the part it already consumed.
And dropping a task's only handle detaches that task instead of stopping it — it just keeps running, completely on its own.
